questions.decision: The submission went out against the original brief even though a mid-flight requirement change was surfaced in the session; no follow-up edits addressed it.
questions.question: Partway through the session a change to the requirements came in. Walk me through what you did when you saw it â€” what did it change about the task in your reading, what did you decide to do about it, and what would the update have cost you to absorb?
questions.listenFor: They can recount the specific change, admit they saw it (or explain honestly why they missed it), and reason concretely about the trade-off of absorbing it late â€” e.g. what they would have re-scoped or cut. A genuine author knows what the stale brief actually said versus the new one.
questions.redFlag: They don't remember any requirement change existing, describe it only in generic terms ('there was an update, I handled the main scope'), or claim they addressed it when the submission shows no corresponding edits.

questions.decision: The 'feel safe' resilience ambiguity (restore-on-reload vs local draft vs warn-before-leave vs tighter flush) was never opened or resolved; no clarifying question was asked either.
questions.question: The brief asked that candidates 'feel safe' about losing work. There are at least three different loss modes you could have targeted â€” losing work on reload, losing an unflushed buffer, or losing local edits to a server restore. Which one did you understand the brief to mean, which would you have built first, and what would make you pick a different one?
questions.listenFor: They can enumerate distinct loss scenarios unprompted, tie each to a concrete mechanism in the editor (flush cadence, unload events, localStorage reconciliation), and give a reasoned first pick with a counterfactual ('if the flush interval were shorter, warn-before-unload matters less').
questions.redFlag: They treat all options as equally fine, can't name a concrete loss scenario, or pivot to describing what the submission contains rather than reasoning about the choice they didn't visibly make.

questions.decision: The existing flush()/re-buffer capture pipeline and its append-only hash-chain event log were left untouched â€” never opened during the session.
questions.question: The session editor already had a flush-and-re-buffer pipeline writing to an append-only event log with an integrity chain. If you had added a restore path, how would you have kept the event log's guarantees intact â€” and what specifically in that existing code would you have had to read first to be sure?
questions.listenFor: They reason about ordering and append-only constraints concretely â€” e.g. a restore must be a read path or a new event type, retries must be idempotent, rewriting past events breaks the chain. Someone who worked in this codebase can name what they'd inspect (the flush function, how the batch re-buffers on failure).
questions.redFlag: They hand-wave ('I'd just make sure not to break it'), propose rewriting the flush loop without acknowledging the re-verification cost, or show no awareness that an integrity contract existed at all despite it being in the code they submitted.

questions.decision: No failure-path verification was observed â€” zero verification asks to the assistant and the retry/restore edge cases were never exercised.
questions.question: Suppose a flush request fails and the client retries. What's the failure mode you'd be most worried about in your submission, and how did you â€” or how would you â€” convince yourself it doesn't happen? Walk me through the actual check, not the intention.
questions.listenFor: They name the double-append hazard (the re-buffered batch getting written twice) or stale-restore-over-newer-edits unprompted, and describe a concrete reproduction: killing the network mid-flush, asserting on event counts, or a test against the real route. Genuine verifiers describe what they observed, not what they hoped.
questions.redFlag: They describe verification as 'I tested it and it worked' with no mechanism, can't name any specific failure mode in their own retry logic, or only propose checks the interviewer just implied.

questions.decision: Three self-authored prompts with iteration depth 3 (briefPasteRatio 0.0) drove the assistant, alongside a 3-entry decision log.
questions.question: Your prompts to the assistant were short and iterative rather than pasting the brief in. Pick the exchange where the assistant's first answer wasn't what you wanted â€” what was wrong with it, and how did you steer the follow-up?
questions.listenFor: They can reconstruct a specific back-and-forth: what the first draft got wrong, the exact correction they gave, and why their phrasing changed. Real iteration leaves a memory of friction â€” a wrong assumption, a missing constraint they had to supply.
questions.redFlag: They can't recall any exchange where the assistant was wrong, describe the interaction only in general terms ('I refined it until it was good'), or the iteration story doesn't match a three-prompt session.

questions.decision: One stakeholder question was asked, but zero clarifying questions about the brief's ambiguities.
questions.question: You went to the stakeholder once during the session. What did you ask, why was that the thing worth spending your one question on, and what did you deliberately decide NOT to ask and resolve on your own instead?
questions.listenFor: They remember the actual question and the answer, can justify its priority over other unknowns, and can name at least one ambiguity they consciously self-resolved with a stated assumption â€” showing the triage was deliberate.
questions.redFlag: They don't remember contacting the stakeholder, invent a plausible-sounding question that doesn't match the record, or frame the brief as having had no ambiguities worth asking about.
